newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq oil deal progresses despite UN succession row.
newsitem.headline: Iraq oil deal progresses despite UN succession row.

text.p: The United Nations-Iraq oil-for-food scheme appears to be making progress toward implementation in the first quarter of 1997, despite the heated battle over the future of U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, diplomats said.

With the U.S. apparently determined to deny Boutros-Ghali a second term, some analysts have speculated that his departure at the end of this year could add to delays which have held up implementation most of this year.

The deal, which allows Iraq to sell up to $2 billion of oil over six months on a renewable basis to pay for humanitarian needs, has been strongly supported by the secretary-general amid close scrutiny and many objections by the United States.

But among the positive signals diplamats point to is the plan to send the Dutch firm Saybolt, charged with monitoring the implementation of the deal on the ground, back to Iraq on December 5 to check the operational status of an oil metering station on the Iraq-Turkey border.
Saybolt inspectors found equipment missing at the Zakho metering station during an early November visit, but Iraq was expected to be replacing the key components.
Also, Lloyds of London personnel will arrive in Iraq next Wednesday to inspect facilities at three points along border areas where humanitarian aid will be imported and monitored.

"If the Saybolt and Lloyds visits go well, we could be headed toward implementation. We could have a report before the end of the year (from the two firms) and be looking at starting in early February," said one Western diplomat.
Diplomats and U.N. officials agreed that if Boutros-Ghali is forced out at the end of his term on December 31, momentum for getting the oil deal finalized should not be affected.
A Western diplomat noted that even if Boutros-Ghali is not re-elected , a new secretary-general would likely have similar views on the subject."
The source said that implementation could actually be expedited if Boutros-Ghali sees his bid for a new term fail.
"I would think he'd want to get this all done before the end of the year, to report the Secretariat has done everything for full implementation," said the diplomat.
Before the parties reach that point, technical problems must be resolved, one of which is acceptance by the U.N. Sanctions Committee on Iraq of a formula for pricing oil contracts.
Iraq's ambassador to the United Nations, Nizar Hamdoom, said his country just submitted a third pricing formula for approval by the U.N. sanctions committee.

"We are waiting for the Americans to approve the third update of the pricing formula," Hamdoon told Reuters on Wednesday. It is "difficult to say (when the oil sales would start), that lies with the American delegation," he said.
The formula covers oil sales in December and would likely be blocked by the U.S. when voted on in the next two weeks, one Sanctions Committee member said.

But U.S. and U.N. officials have said that the price formula is irrelevant until more fundamental issues are resolved. For example, Iraq must clarify and change its demand that Baghdad control the number and make-up of U.N. observers stationed in the country, one U.N. official said.

"These practical issues have to be resolved. The U.N. will hire the local observers, not Iraq, and we will determine the number of observers. We also have to be guaranteed freedom of movement. There is no way Baghdad will submit a list of personnel," he said.
